Part 3 is the reproduction. Three of the five Multi100 analysts fitted their models on means of countries or of cells, and the results recorded for the three come back to the third decimal from files that the browser lab already holds. You choose one of the three. The other two worked on respondents, and their reproduction needs the respondent files that only a GESIS account can give, so it belongs to the three-day course. The part ends on what the reproduction took and on the code that your analyst deposited, and it takes ninety minutes.

## 1. The instruction of Multi100

**On the slides.** The slides read the four instructions of the second Multi100 task word for word and say what each of them assumes. The slides then show the columns of the panel and the three analyses that can be reproduced on aggregate data, and set the aim of the part, in which you become analyst no. 6.

## 2. Task 3 – The reproduction

[Open the browser lab at Task 3](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-3-reproduction){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Choose one analyst and fill the gaps in its cell, which has a hint and a full solution under it. The first run of the cell of 018OL downloads two packages, about 32 MB. When you have the value on record, type the analyst and the value in the chat, for example `KQXUE t = -7.169`, hold it, and send it when the facilitator says go. If you finish early, take a second analyst. In the workspace, the working script holds the same three analyses.

| Analyst | Data | Model | Recorded by Multi100 |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| C6HJR | the course panel, `EUframes_cy.csv`, 270 country-years | fixed effects for country and year, conventional standard errors | t = −3.804 on 233 df |
| KQXUE | `analyst_KQXUE.csv`, 270 country-years | a fixed effect for each country, conventional standard errors | t = −7.169 on 242 df |
| 018OL | `analyst_018OL.csv`, 420 cells of country, year and wave | random intercepts for country, year and wave, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom | t = −1.206 on 396.9 df |

The two files of KQXUE and 018OL were rebuilt by the course from the GESIS waves, following the code that each analyst deposited, and the [codebook](../../cases/eu-frames/data/analyst_panels_codebook.md) of the two files says how.

## 3. Reproducibility and analytical choice

**On the slides.** The slides explain why everyone who chose the same analyst got the same t, and why the three analysts did not get the same t as one another.

## 4. What a reproduction needs

**On the slides.** A reproduction needs the data, the code and the right versions of both, and the slides give the example of a value of a Eurostat series that was revised after the analyst used it. The slides then set out the slips that three of the five pipelines carry, and what each slip does to the t.

## 5. Hands-on 3b – Reading deposited code

[KQXUE, `task2.do`](https://osf.io/vycgd/){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"} [018OL, the R Markdown file of Task 2](https://osf.io/nz7ka/){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"} [C6HJR, the folder of April 2025](https://osf.io/6zqct/){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

Open the OSF deposit of the analyst whom you reproduced and find the line that carries the slip. Then write one check that would have caught it, hold it, and send it when the facilitator says go. Before the break, copy your Task 3 cell and its output into your notes, because the browser lab forgets everything when it reloads.

**By the end of the part** you have reproduced a recorded result to the third decimal, you know what it took besides the code, and you have written a check that would have caught the slip in the pipeline of your analyst.
